items.prompt: A three-tier application has a web tier, stateless API tier, transactional data, and a search feature. Which selection method avoids choosing services by popularity alone?
constraints: Each tier has a different workload contract.
The team wants managed operations.
The design must preserve data and availability requirements.

options.text: Translate each tier into access pattern, consistency, latency, durability, scale, security, and operations requirements, then select the narrowest managed service that satisfies the contract.
Use one database and one EC2 instance for all tiers because fewer service names always means lower risk.
Choose the newest managed service for every tier without measuring the workload or support boundary.
Choose services from subnet type alone because private placement determines data-model fit.

feedback.Reason: Purpose-built selection starts with workload contracts, not generic service popularity or infrastructure placement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Managed services optimize for particular data models, access patterns, scaling behavior, and operations. The architect maps requirements before comparing service boundaries and limitations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team uses a stateless compute tier, a transactional store, a search index, and separate object or file storage only where the workload needs them.
Details.errorCorrection: One instance creates shared failure and scaling coupling, newest does not mean fit, and subnet type does not determine data semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More purpose-built services improve fit but add integration and governance surface; each service needs an owner and recovery plan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Fewer components can create larger failure, scaling, and data-model coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Service novelty is not evidence of workload fit or operational maturity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network placement affects reachability and security, not whether a data model supports the workload.

items.prompt: An order system requires joins, foreign keys, multi-row transactions, and a mature SQL reporting ecosystem. Which data service family should be evaluated first?
constraints: Transactional integrity is required.
The application has relational access patterns.
The team prefers managed database operations.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon RDS or Aurora with an engine and configuration that support the required SQL, transaction, compatibility, backup, and availability contract.
Choose DynamoDB because every relational join and multi-row transaction is transparent through a key-value API.
Choose S3 because objects provide foreign keys and transactional joins when versioning is enabled.
Choose ElastiCache as the system of record because cached values provide durable relational constraints.

feedback.Reason: Relational engines are the natural candidate when joins, relational constraints, SQL compatibility, and transactional semantics are central requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS and Aurora provide managed relational database engines with engine-specific features, backups, scaling, and high-availability choices.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates engine compatibility, connection behavior, Multi-AZ and backup requirements, and the workload's read and write profile.
Details.errorCorrection: DynamoDB uses a different access model, S3 objects do not provide relational joins, and a cache is not a durable source of truth.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Relational fit may trade some horizontal scale simplicity for transaction and query capability; the chosen engine still needs capacity and recovery design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DynamoDB requires access-pattern modeling and does not transparently provide arbitrary relational joins.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 is object storage and does not provide foreign keys or database transactions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: ElastiCache is an acceleration layer and should not be the authoritative transactional store.

items.prompt: A session service needs single-digit-millisecond lookups by user ID, predictable key-based writes, and very high horizontal scale without joins. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: The access pattern is known in advance.
The workload is key-value oriented.
Managed scaling is preferred.

options.text: Evaluate DynamoDB with a key design, capacity mode, consistency choice, TTL, and conditional-write model that match the session workload.
Use RDS and add a join for every session read because relational normalization is required for all key-value workloads.
Use S3 and scan objects by user ID for every request because object storage automatically indexes arbitrary fields.
Use CloudFront as the authoritative session database because edge caches always persist user state durably.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB is purpose-built for key-value and document access patterns with managed horizontal scale and configurable consistency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB tables require primary-key and access-pattern design; capacity, indexes, TTL, consistency, and conditional operations are part of the workload contract.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team chooses a partition key with sufficient distribution, sets expiration for sessions, and validates hot-key and retry behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: RDS can fit other requirements but adds unnecessary relational overhead here, S3 is not a per-request arbitrary-field index, and CloudFront cache state is not an authoritative durable store.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DynamoDB requires deliberate key modeling and has service-specific limits; arbitrary ad hoc queries may need another data model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Relational joins are not required for a known key-value session access pattern.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 does not provide a low-latency arbitrary-field lookup for every object request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Edge cache entries are not the durable authoritative session database.

items.prompt: A product catalog is read thousands of times more often than it changes, and database latency is now the dominant API cost. Which tier should be added without making the cache the source of truth?
constraints: Catalog reads can tolerate bounded staleness.
The database remains authoritative.
Cache misses must still return correct data.

options.text: Evaluate ElastiCache or an appropriate application cache with an explicit invalidation or TTL strategy, cache-aside behavior, and a database fallback.
Move the only catalog copy into the cache and delete the database because cache hits are faster.
Use a security group as a read cache because network rules are evaluated faster than database queries.
Disable expiration so stale catalog entries never cause a cache miss.

feedback.Reason: A managed cache can reduce repeated reads while the durable database remains the source of truth and cache freshness is explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ElastiCache supports in-memory caching patterns; the application chooses cache-aside, write-through, invalidation, or TTL behavior and handles misses and stale values.
Details.scenarioApplication: The API checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, populates a bounded entry, and invalidates or expires entries after catalog changes.
Details.errorCorrection: A cache alone is not durable authority, security groups do not store values, and never-expiring entries can serve indefinitely stale data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Caching improves latency and database load but adds invalidation complexity, memory cost, and a stale-read contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A cache failure or eviction would lose the only catalog copy and violate durability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups contain network rules and no cached application data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unbounded freshness can create correctness failures when catalog data changes.

items.prompt: A catalog API needs full-text search, relevance ranking, tokenization, and faceted filtering across denormalized documents. Which managed service family should be evaluated?
constraints: Search is a derived view, not the transactional source.
The workload needs text analysis and ranking.
Index rebuild or replay is possible.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon OpenSearch Service for the search index, keep the transactional source authoritative, and design indexing, refresh, scaling, and rebuild behavior explicitly.
Use a security group because it can evaluate text relevance before traffic reaches the database.
Use S3 prefix listing as the full-text relevance engine for every query.
Use a cache as the only search store and assume evictions never remove indexed documents.

feedback.Reason: OpenSearch is purpose-built for search and analytics over indexed documents, while the business source remains separate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: OpenSearch indexes documents for text analysis, queries, ranking, and aggregations. The application must feed the index and handle lag, failures, and rebuilds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The catalog service emits changes, an indexer updates OpenSearch, and a replay path reconstructs the index from authoritative catalog data.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups do not rank text, S3 prefixes are not full-text search, and cache eviction can remove data and cannot be the only index.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Search indexes add operational and consistency boundaries; stale or unavailable search results need an explicit product behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security groups authorize network traffic and do not implement relevance or text analysis.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 prefix listing is object navigation, not full-text ranking and faceting.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache eviction and failure make an in-memory cache unsuitable as the sole durable search index.

items.prompt: A media tier stores large immutable objects, needs durable access from many consumers, and does not require block updates inside an object. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: Objects are read and written as complete objects.
Durability and lifecycle matter.
The workload does not need a shared POSIX filesystem.

options.text: Use Amazon S3 with appropriate bucket policy, encryption, lifecycle, versioning, and access controls for the object contract.
Use an EBS volume shared by every consumer because block storage is the natural model for immutable objects.
Use ElastiCache as the durable media repository because in-memory reads are faster.
Use an RDS table with one row per byte because relational storage is required for every durable payload.

feedback.Reason: S3 is purpose-built for durable object storage, broad access, lifecycle, and object-level controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 stores objects with bucket and object-key semantics, supports storage classes, lifecycle, versioning, encryption, access policies, and event integrations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team uploads media to private S3, uses least-privilege access or signed requests, and applies retention and lifecycle policies.
Details.errorCorrection: EBS is block storage tied to volumes, ElastiCache is not durable media storage, and byte-per-row databases add needless cost and complexity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: S3 object access differs from POSIX or block semantics; clients must use object APIs and handle multipart, metadata, and eventual workflow behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EBS provides block volumes and is not the natural shared immutable object store for many consumers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An in-memory cache is not a durable media repository.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A relational row-per-byte design is inefficient and does not match object access semantics.

items.prompt: Several Linux containers need concurrent access to a shared POSIX directory across Availability Zones, and the data must survive task replacement. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: POSIX file semantics are required.
Multiple tasks need concurrent mounts.
The file data is durable application state.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon EFS with mount targets, security groups, throughput, performance mode, access points, and backup or lifecycle settings matched to the workload.
Use each task's local filesystem because containers in one cluster automatically share files.
Use S3 because object keys provide transparent POSIX locking and directory semantics.
Use an EBS volume attached to every task without checking multi-attach or filesystem coordination.

feedback.Reason: EFS is designed for shared file access across compute resources and Availability Zones when its performance and access model fit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS provides a regional file system with mount targets and NFS access. Security groups, access points, throughput, performance, and lifecycle choices remain part of the design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team mounts EFS privately, scopes access by access point and task identity, tests concurrent file behavior, and monitors throughput.
Details.errorCorrection: Task-local files are isolated, S3 is object storage rather than POSIX, and shared EBS attachment requires explicit supported semantics and coordination.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Shared files can become a contention or locking bottleneck; a service-specific object or database model may scale better for some workloads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Tasks do not share local files merely because they use one cluster.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 does not transparently provide POSIX file and locking semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Multi-attach and filesystem coordination cannot be assumed for every EBS and task arrangement.

items.prompt: A Windows application requires SMB shares, Active Directory integration, and Windows file semantics while moving from a file server. Which managed service should be evaluated?
constraints: The application expects SMB and Windows behavior.
Directory integration is required.
The team wants a managed file service.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with the required Active Directory, network, throughput, backup, and availability configuration.
Use S3 because every Windows application can mount an object bucket as a transparent SMB share without changes.
Use EFS because it provides Windows SMB and Active Directory semantics identically to FSx for Windows.
Use DynamoDB because key-value tables replace filesystem paths and file locks automatically.

feedback.Reason: FSx for Windows File Server is designed for Windows file workloads and SMB or Active Directory integration.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for Windows provides managed Windows file systems with SMB and directory integration options. Network, authentication, throughput, and backup still require design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team joins the file system to the intended directory, places it privately, scopes SMB access, and tests failover and application locking.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 object access is not transparent SMB, EFS is NFS-oriented rather than identical Windows SMB, and DynamoDB is not a file system.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A managed file service reduces server operations but preserves file-system capacity, permissions, and application locking concerns.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 does not transparently provide the SMB filesystem semantics expected by a Windows application.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EFS and FSx for Windows expose different protocols and directory integration models.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DynamoDB does not provide paths, file locks, or filesystem semantics.

items.prompt: An ingestion tier must accept ordered events from many producers, allow multiple independent consumers to replay records, and process data continuously. Which service family should be evaluated?
constraints: The workload is streaming rather than one request per message.
Consumers need independent offsets or replay.
Throughput and retention are explicit requirements.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with shard or on-demand capacity, retention, partition-key distribution, consumer model, and downstream processing design.
Use SQS Standard because it preserves one ordered stream for every independent consumer automatically.
Use an Application Load Balancer as the durable replayable event log.
Use S3 lifecycle rules as the low-latency stream consumer scheduler.

feedback.Reason: Kinesis Data Streams is purpose-built for durable streaming records, partitioned throughput, multiple consumers, and replay within retention.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis streams organize records by partition key and retain them for configured periods while consumers track positions. Capacity and hot partitions are part of the design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team chooses a partition key with even distribution, sets retention and consumer concurrency, and monitors iterator age and throughput.
Details.errorCorrection: SQS Standard does not provide one replayable ordered stream to every consumer, load balancers are not event logs, and lifecycle rules do not schedule stream processing.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Streaming adds partition, retention, consumer lag, and duplicate-processing responsibilities; a queue or object event may fit simpler workloads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SQS Standard is a queue-delivery model and does not provide the stated independent replayable stream semantics by default.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An ALB distributes requests and does not retain a replayable event log.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lifecycle manages objects and does not provide low-latency stream consumption.

items.prompt: The application tier is stateless and scales horizontally, while the data tier needs backups, failover, and schema ownership. Which boundary is strongest?
constraints: Application instances are replaceable.
Data must outlive compute.
The two tiers scale and fail differently.

options.text: Keep application compute and durable data as separate managed or explicitly owned tiers, with a clear API, connection, backup, and failure contract between them.
Store the database inside every application container so scaling the app automatically replicates authoritative data.
Use a single shared local volume for every application and database process without backup or ownership rules.
Use a load balancer as the database because it already distributes application traffic.

feedback.Reason: Separating stateless compute from durable data preserves independent scaling, recovery, ownership, and lifecycle.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Managed database and storage services provide durability and recovery capabilities distinct from task or instance lifecycle. The application tier connects through explicit endpoints and least-privilege credentials.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team scales the API without copying database state into tasks and tests database failover, connection recovery, and application retry behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Per-container databases create conflicting authority, shared local volumes do not automatically provide durable managed recovery, and load balancers are not databases.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate tiers add network latency and connection management but avoid coupling compute replacement to data durability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Scaling application tasks does not create a safe replicated database or authoritative write model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A shared local volume does not provide the required backup, failover, and ownership semantics by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A load balancer distributes traffic and cannot store transactional data.

items.prompt: The API team wants to query billing tables directly from the application tier, but billing is owned by another service with a separate schema lifecycle. What should change?
constraints: Billing data has one business owner.
The API needs only a defined read view.
Schema changes must not require synchronized application deploys.

options.text: Expose a billing-owned API or read projection with a versioned contract, and prevent the API tier from depending on billing's internal tables.
Grant the API broad database access because direct SQL is always faster than a service contract.
Copy every billing table into the API container image so schema changes are local.
Use an ALB listener rule to authorize access to individual database tables.

feedback.Reason: Data ownership and contract boundaries prevent a consumer from coupling to another service's storage implementation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A service can publish a stable API or projection while retaining schema ownership. Consumers can tolerate versioning and eventual consistency according to the business requirement.
Details.scenarioApplication: Billing exposes the required fields, the API uses least-privilege access, and contract tests detect intended changes without sharing tables.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct broad SQL creates schema and security coupling, images are not live data stores, and ALB rules do not authorize database columns.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A projection may be slightly stale but preserves autonomy; a synchronous API may be appropriate when the read must be current and bounded.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct database access couples the API to schema and broadens the data blast radius.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An image cannot hold live billing data or provide a safe update contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Load-balancer routing rules do not authorize database table access.

items.prompt: A workload writes immutable event records once, reads them by object key or time range, and rarely updates individual records. Which storage model is most aligned?
constraints: Records are append-oriented.
Reads can use key or partition conventions.
Per-record transactional updates are not central.

options.text: Evaluate an object or append-oriented service such as S3 or a streaming store based on retention, query, replay, and consumer requirements rather than forcing a relational update model.
Use a relational database row update for every immutable record because all workloads benefit from mutable normalization.
Use an in-memory cache as the only record store because writes are infrequent.
Use a security group to partition event records by time range.

feedback.Reason: Append-oriented immutable records often fit object or streaming storage better than a transactional update-centric database.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 provides object durability and lifecycle; Kinesis provides ordered partitioned streams and retention. Selection depends on access, replay, query, and freshness needs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses S3 for durable objects or Kinesis for active stream consumption, then defines partitioning, retention, and processing.
Details.errorCorrection: A relational row can work but may add unnecessary update and capacity semantics, a cache is not durable authority, and network rules do not partition data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Object and stream services optimize for different retrieval and processing patterns; an analytics query tier may be needed for ad hoc analysis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Relational storage is not automatically the best fit for immutable append records and may add unnecessary complexity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cache data can be evicted and should not be the sole durable record store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups control traffic and do not partition application records.

items.prompt: A team chooses a managed database to reduce host patching but has not assigned ownership for schema migrations, credentials, backups, restore tests, or query performance. What remains true?
constraints: AWS manages some infrastructure layers.
The application still owns data and schema behavior.
Recovery requirements are explicit.

options.text: Document the shared-responsibility boundary: AWS manages the service infrastructure, while the team still owns schema, data access, credentials, backups or restore validation, queries, and application recovery behavior.
Assume managed means AWS owns all data loss, schema, query, and application recovery decisions automatically.
Remove application backups because a managed service cannot be deleted accidentally.
Give every developer database administrator access because managed services remove security risk from credentials.

feedback.Reason: Managed services reduce infrastructure operations but do not transfer application, data, identity, and recovery responsibilities wholesale.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The service provider manages the underlying service according to its model; customers configure access, data protection, backups, retention, schema, workload capacity, and recovery tests.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team assigns owners, rotates credentials, validates backup restores, monitors queries, and rehearses the application failover path.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed does not mean deletion-proof or schema-aware, and broad developer access increases risk rather than removing it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Less host maintenance is exchanged for service-specific limits and configuration responsibility; the boundary must be visible in runbooks.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Managed infrastructure does not make all data, schema, query, or application decisions automatic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Managed services can still be misconfigured or deleted; backups and restore validation remain required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed status does not justify broad database administrator access.

items.prompt: A service requires multi-AZ database availability, automatic replacement, and a tested restore path, but its current single container database fails during host maintenance. Which change is strongest?
constraints: Data must survive compute replacement.
The service has an availability objective.
Application connections can be adapted to a managed endpoint.

options.text: Move the durable database responsibility to a managed multi-AZ service or explicitly operated highly available data tier, then test connection recovery, failover, backups, and restore.
Run two independent database containers with no replication or conflict strategy because two copies always provide availability.
Place the single database container in a public subnet so maintenance cannot interrupt it.
Add more application replicas while leaving the single database failure point unchanged.

feedback.Reason: Application replicas do not remove a single stateful database failure point; the data tier needs its own availability and recovery design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Managed relational services can provide multi-AZ failover and backups according to selected options. Application code must reconnect and recovery must be tested rather than assumed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team selects an appropriate data service, keeps it private, configures backups, and verifies behavior during failover and restore.
Details.errorCorrection: Unreplicated copies can diverge, public placement does not prevent maintenance failure, and extra app replicas do not make one database highly available.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed availability has cost and engine limitations; the architecture must still define acceptable failover time and data loss.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Two uncoordinated databases can diverge and do not constitute a safe failover design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public placement increases exposure and does not prevent maintenance or host failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Scaling stateless compute does not remove the single database failure domain.

items.prompt: A managed service stores customer data and is reachable from a private application tier. Which security controls must remain part of the architecture?
constraints: The service is managed by AWS.
Customer data has access and encryption requirements.
The application uses workload identities.

options.text: Define least-privilege IAM or resource policies, private network access where supported, encryption and key ownership, secret rotation, audit logging, and data-retention controls for the service.
Assume managed services are public by default and rely only on the application's input validation.
Use a security group as the complete data authorization model for an object or database service.
Disable encryption because the service provider already protects the underlying hardware.

feedback.Reason: Managed service status does not eliminate customer responsibility for identity, data access, encryption, network exposure, logging, or retention.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Service-specific IAM, resource policies, endpoint controls, KMS or service-managed encryption, and audit events implement different layers of protection.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team grants the workload only required actions, uses private endpoints or subnets, rotates secrets, and monitors access and configuration changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed services are not automatically public or authorized, security groups do not replace data policy, and hardware protection does not satisfy application encryption requirements.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More controls add configuration and key-management work, but the data classification and threat model determine which are mandatory.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Managed services still require explicit access and exposure controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are network filters and do not define all IAM or resource-level data permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Provider hardware protection does not replace encryption and key or access requirements.

items.prompt: The API tier scales from 10 to 1,000 tasks during campaigns, but the relational data tier cannot accept 1,000 new connections. Which managed-service design protects the bottleneck?
constraints: Compute can scale much faster than the database.
Connection count is a hard limit.
The application can use pooling or a proxy.

options.text: Bound application concurrency, use appropriate connection pooling or RDS Proxy where supported, and scale the data tier and cache deliberately rather than letting compute fan out unbounded connections.
Allow every new task to open unlimited database connections because managed databases scale automatically with clients.
Put the database behind CloudFront because edge caching creates database connections only when the cache misses.
Increase the API container image size so the database accepts more connections per task.

feedback.Reason: Independent elasticity can overwhelm a slower data tier; connection and concurrency controls must align the tiers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Database connection limits and transaction capacity are distinct from compute task count. Pooling, proxying, caching, queueing, and bounded concurrency reduce connection storms.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team sets a connection budget per task, uses a proxy or pool, caps scaling from downstream capacity, and monitors saturation and queue age.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed databases have limits, CloudFront is not a general database connection proxy, and image size does not affect connection capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Capping compute can increase request latency during bursts; asynchronous buffering or a purpose-built data model may be needed for the SLO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Managed databases still have finite connections and transaction capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront caching does not provide a general connection-pooling boundary for private database clients.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Image size has no relationship to database connection capacity.

items.prompt: A team is building its own durable queue, retry scheduler, and dead-letter processor for a workload that has no unique messaging semantics. What decision should be challenged?
constraints: The workload can use standard queue semantics.
The team has limited platform capacity.
Reliability and operations matter more than custom implementation.

options.text: Evaluate a managed queue and messaging service first, then build custom infrastructure only for a demonstrated requirement that the managed service cannot satisfy.
Continue building because custom queue code always has lower operational cost than a managed service.
Use a database table as a queue without defining visibility, retry, poison-message, or concurrency semantics.
Use a security group as the durable message buffer because it is already provisioned for the application.

feedback.Reason: Purpose-built managed services can remove undifferentiated reliability and scaling work when their contract fits the workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS and related services provide durable delivery, visibility, retry, and DLQ mechanisms. A custom queue inherits all of those correctness and operational responsibilities.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team compares throughput, ordering, latency, retention, cost, and integration requirements, then uses a managed queue if no custom guarantee is needed.
Details.errorCorrection: Custom infrastructure is not automatically cheaper, an ad hoc database queue hides missing semantics, and security groups cannot buffer messages.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A managed service may constrain semantics or quotas; custom code is justified only when that constraint is material and the team can operate it safely.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Custom queue code carries storage, duplicate, retry, scaling, and recovery costs that managed services already address.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A database table does not automatically provide queue visibility, delivery, and poison-message semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups are network policies and cannot store or deliver messages.

items.prompt: Two managed services both satisfy the functional API, but one has the required Region availability and backup model while the other has lower unit price. Which evidence should decide?
constraints: The architecture has a recovery requirement.
The service must be available in the deployment Regions.
Cost matters only after mandatory constraints are met.

options.text: Eliminate options that fail mandatory Region, durability, backup, security, or recovery requirements, then compare cost, operations, performance, and integration trade-offs among the remaining services.
Choose the lower unit price because all managed services provide identical durability and regional coverage.
Choose the service with the most features even when the required recovery model is unavailable in the target Region.
Choose from the service logo because brand familiarity is stronger evidence than the workload contract.

feedback.Reason: Architecture selection is constraint-first: a cheaper or more feature-rich option is invalid when it fails mandatory availability or recovery requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Service capabilities vary by Region, mode, quota, backup, security, and integration. A decision record should separate hard constraints from weighted trade-offs and cite current official limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team verifies Region and recovery support, rejects the noncompliant option, and then compares cost and operational fit for the viable service.
Details.errorCorrection: Unit price does not prove equal durability, feature count cannot compensate for a missing mandatory recovery model, and brand is not workload evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Service limits and regional availability can change, so the decision must be revalidated before activation and during major architecture changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Lower price cannot make an option satisfy a failed mandatory architecture constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Extra features do not compensate for unavailable recovery or regional support.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Brand familiarity is not evidence of fit, availability, or operational behavior.
